title: Parcel With Few Handoffs
story: You run a small pottery shop and ship a fragile vase through a network of courier depots. Each route between two depots is run by a different small firm, goes one way only, and has its own fee. Chaining cheap routes together is usually the best deal.

But every time the parcel stops at a depot in between, it is unloaded and reloaded, and that is when vases break. So you allow at most maxStops stops between the depot where you drop it off and the depot where the buyer collects it. What is the cheapest way to send it under that rule?
task: Write cheapestDelivery(n, routes, origin, dest, maxStops). Depots are numbered 0 to n - 1. Each [a, b, fee] in routes is a one-way route from depot a to depot b. Return the lowest total fee to get from origin to dest passing through at most maxStops depots in between.
A direct route has 0 stops. A trip using 3 routes has 2 stops. Return -1 if no trip within the limit exists.
constraints: 0 ≤ a, b < n and a ≠ b; no route is listed twice

examples.explanation: The cheapest trip overall is 0 → 1 → 2 → 3 for 30, but it stops twice. With at most 1 stop, the choices are 0 → 3 for 50 and 0 → 2 → 3 for 35. The answer is 35.
The only trip stops at depot 1, and no stops are allowed. Return -1.

hints: In the first example, what is the cheapest fee to reach each depot using exactly 1 route? Using at most 2 routes? How does the second list follow from the first?
"At most k stops" is the same as "at most k + 1 routes". Think in rounds: after round r, you know the cheapest fee to every depot using at most r routes.

To go from round r to round r + 1, try extending every round-r trip by one more route. There is a trap: if you update the fees in place while going through the routes, a single round can chain several routes. How do you prevent that?

Run Bellman-Ford for exactly maxStops + 1 rounds. In each round, copy the current fee array, then for every route [a, b, fee] update copy[b] using the old value of a. Replace the array with the copy at the end of the round. The answer is the fee at dest, or -1 if it is still infinite.
bruteForce: Try every trip of up to maxStops + 1 routes with a depth-first search, and keep the cheapest that ends at dest. With many routes out of each depot, the number of trips grows like (routes per depot)stops, so a dense network with 99 allowed stops is far out of reach.
Plain Dijkstra is fast but wrong here. It keeps only the cheapest fee per depot and throws away a pricier path that used fewer stops, which may be the only one still allowed to reach dest.

walkthrough: The limit on stops is really a limit on the number of routes: at most maxStops + 1. Bellman-Ford naturally counts routes. Each round extends every known trip by one route, so after round r the array holds the cheapest fee using at most r routes. Stop after maxStops + 1 rounds.
Trace the first example with maxStops = 1, so 2 rounds. Fees start as [0, ∞, ∞, ∞].
• Round 1, reading [0, ∞, ∞, ∞]. From depot 0: depot 1 = 10, depot 3 = 50, depot 2 = 25. Routes out of 1 and 2 are skipped because their old fees are ∞. Result [0, 10, 25, 50].
• Round 2, reading [0, 10, 25, 50]. 1 → 2 gives 20, better than 25. 2 → 3 gives 25 + 10 = 35, better than 50. Result [0, 10, 20, 35].

The answer is 35. Notice that round 2 used depot 2's old fee, 25, not the fresh 20. The 20 comes from 0 → 1 → 2, which already used 2 routes, so adding 2 → 3 would make 3 routes. Reading from the old array is exactly what enforces the limit.

That copy is the whole difficulty. Update in place and, when routes happen to be listed in path order, one round can run along a whole chain. The test with routes 0→1→2→3 and no stops allowed catches it: in place, you would return 3 instead of 100.
solution.timeWhy: k = maxStops + 1 rounds, each looking at all m routes once.
solution.spaceWhy: Two fee arrays of length n.
solution.takeaway: When a shortest path is limited to at most k edges, run k rounds of Bellman-Ford, and read each round from a copy of the previous one. Round r then holds exactly the best costs using at most r edges.
